summary: Delivery status notifications are limited to ASCII in their machine-readable parts. This RFC adds a new address type for internationalized email addresses so the original recipient with non-ASCII characters is preserved in delivery and disposition notifications.

plainLanguage.summary: When a letter cannot be delivered, a note comes back. This makes sure the note can write the name correctly even when it has letters from other alphabets.

questions: what is a delivery status notification
how do bounce messages handle non-ascii addresses
what is the utf-8 address type in dsn
subtitle: How bounce messages and read receipts keep the original recipient address when it contains non-ASCII characters.

tldr.problem: Delivery status notifications and message disposition notifications only allow ASCII text in their machine-readable parts, so an email address with non-ASCII characters cannot be reported correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a UTF-8 address type with three forms, and defines three new UTF-8 media types for the status report, the returned message and the returned headers, plus one for disposition notifications.
tldr.outcome: A sender can match each notification to the recipient address it originally used, even after a message was downgraded along the way. This is a Standards Track revision of the experimental RFC 5337.

today: RFC 6533 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 5337 and updates RFC 3461, RFC 3464, RFC 3798 and RFC 6522. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Notifications Need UTF-8
sections.content:
When a message is sent with the SMTPUTF8 extension and internationalized headers, it may need to be returned, or it may trigger a Message Disposition Notification (MDN). A message sent to several recipients can produce a notification for each one, so it helps if the client can match each notification to the recipient address it originally gave. That means the original recipient has to be preserved.

The existing formats for delivery status notifications (DSNs) are limited to ASCII in their machine-readable parts. This RFC describes how to preserve the original recipient and updates the DSN and MDN formats to carry the new address types.

It is a revision of and replacement for the experimental RFC 5337. The names of the UTF-8 address type and of the media types message/global, message/global-delivery-status and message/global-headers did not change.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone's name uses letters from another alphabet, the returned note must be able to write that name exactly. This RFC teaches the note-writing system how.

sections.title: The UTF-8 Address Type
sections.content:
RFC 3464 defines the idea of an address type. This RFC adds a UTF-8 address type with three forms: utf-8-addr-xtext, utf-8-addr-unitext and utf-8-address. Only the first is 7-bit safe, meaning it uses only ASCII characters.

An SMTP server that advertises both SMTPUTF8 and the DSN extension MUST accept a UTF-8 address type in the ORCPT parameter, including 8-bit UTF-8 characters. The plain utf-8-address form MUST NOT be used in ORCPT when the server does not advertise SMTPUTF8, when the address contains ASCII characters the parameter forbids (such as a space or =), or in a 7-bit transport environment. In those cases the 7-bit form must be used instead.

The unitext encoding writes characters outside ASCII, and also control characters, space, \, + and =, as \x{HEXPOINT}, where HEXPOINT is 2 to 6 hexadecimal digits. When sending to a server that supports SMTPUTF8, native UTF-8 characters SHOULD be used instead. When the server does not advertise it, the \x{...} syntax MUST be used. The RFC calls this encoding a transitional mechanism to avoid where possible.

When an ORCPT value is copied into an Original-Recipient: field of a message/global-delivery-status part, it SHOULD be converted to the utf-8-address form by removing the unitext encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to write a foreign-alphabet address. One uses only plain letters and codes so it can travel through old mail machines, and the others use the real letters when the machines can handle them.

sections.title: UTF-8 Delivery Status Notifications
sections.content:
A traditional DSN is a three-part multipart/report: human-readable text, a 7-bit-only message/delivery-status, and an optional third part with the returned content or headers. Because that format cannot return an undeliverable SMTPUTF8 message, three media types are used.

  • message/global-delivery-status has the syntax of message/delivery-status with three changes: its charset is UTF-8, so any field MAY contain UTF-8; generators SHOULD use the utf-8-address form for addresses with non-ASCII characters; and an optional Localized-Diagnostic: field is added.
  • message/global returns the content, like message/rfc822 but with UTF-8 headers (described in RFC 6532).
  • message/global-headers returns only the UTF-8 header fields of the message.

Each Localized-Diagnostic: field carries a language tag and text in that language, equivalent to the text part of Diagnostic-Code:. All instances MUST use different language tags. The Diagnostic-Code: field SHOULD be in the i-default language.

For a multipart/report container, the three new types MUST be treated as equivalent to message/delivery-status, message/rfc822 and text/rfc822-headers, so implementations MUST expect any combination of the six. The new types will typically use the 8bit Content-Transfer-Encoding. If all content is 7-bit, the traditional types MAY be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The returned note comes in three parts: what went wrong, the original letter and its envelope. Each part now has a version that can hold foreign-alphabet letters, and the note can even explain the problem in several languages.

sections.title: Rules for SMTP Servers
sections.content:
If an SMTP server that advertises both SMTPUTF8 and DSN must return an undeliverable SMTPUTF8 message, it has two choices for wrapping that message in the multipart/report.

If the return-path SMTP server does not support SMTPUTF8, the undeliverable body part and headers MUST be encoded with a 7-bit Content-Transfer-Encoding such as base64 or quoted-printable. Otherwise, 8bit can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: If the next mailbox cannot read special letters, the returned letter is packed in a plain-letters wrapper first. If it can, the letter goes back as it is.

sections.title: UTF-8 Message Disposition Notifications
sections.content:
MDNs (RFC 3798) have a similar design to DSNs and use the same return format. For a UTF-8 header message, the third part of the multipart/report holds the returned content (message/global) or headers (message/global-headers). The second part uses a new type, message/global-disposition-notification.

That type has the syntax of message/disposition-notification with two changes. Its charset is UTF-8, so fields such as Failure, Error and Warning MAY contain UTF-8 (and SHOULD be in the i-default language). And systems generating it, typically a mail user agent, SHOULD use the UTF-8 address type for addresses with non-ASCII characters.

A delivery agent writing an Original-Recipient: header in native UTF-8 format SHOULD convert the xtext or unitext form from the ORCPT parameter to the matching utf-8-address form. The Disposition-Notification-To: header follows the same 8-bit rules as From: and To:.
sections.plainLanguage: Read receipts get the same upgrade. The note that says a letter was read can now use real foreign-alphabet letters too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using these reports automatically without authentication is risky. Forged negative reports can enable denial-of-service attacks when reports maintain directories or mailing lists, and forged positive reports may make a sender believe a message was delivered when it was not. Malicious users can also craft report structures to trigger coding flaws in parsers, so parsers need secure coding techniques and code review.

Messages with forged return paths cause a large amount of unwanted "blowback" traffic, and many users ignore delivery status notifications as a result. The RFC says correlating notifications with sent messages has become a critical feature of mail clients. In the short term, matching Message-IDs may be enough; in the longer term, cryptographic signature material that securely ties the notification to the original message is advisable. Because UTF-8 is now allowed in more fields, the security considerations of RFC 3629 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can send a fake "your letter did not arrive" note. So mail programs should check that a note really matches a letter they sent.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC creates no new IANA registries, but it registers several items: the UTF-8 mail address type, an update to the smtp diagnostic type registration (replacing the one from RFC 5337), and the media types message/global-headers, message/global-delivery-status and message/global-disposition-notification.
sections.plainLanguage: The new names are written in the official list so everyone uses them the same way.
